lead: Every real process generates entropy, and that entropy generation carries a work penalty. With surroundings at temperature T₀, take work input as positive. The ideal work of a steady-flow unit is W<sub>ideal</sub> = ΔH − T₀ΔS. When W<sub>ideal</sub> is negative the unit produces work, and the best work it can give is −W<sub>ideal</sub> = T₀ΔS − ΔH. The difference W<sub>actual</sub> − W<sub>ideal</sub> is the lost work, W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>. Power plants, refrigerators and heat-recovery networks use this number to see where useful work is thrown away.
prereq: You need entropy, entropy generation and the entropy balance from entropy and the Clausius inequality and control-volume entropy balance, plus the steady-flow energy balance from the first-law chapters.

sections.h3: Ideal work and the dead state

blocks.text: Take the surroundings as a large reservoir at temperature T₀. T₀ is the dead-state temperature: heat exchanged with the environment at T₀ has zero work potential. The ideal work imagines the same change of state done with no entropy generation: any heat the stream must gain or lose is passed through reversible engines or heat pumps that work against the surroundings at T₀.

For a steady-flow unit with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, take work input as positive and write W<sub>ideal</sub> = ΔH − T₀ΔS. Here ΔH is outlet minus inlet enthalpy in kJ, ΔS is outlet minus inlet entropy in kJ/K, and T₀ is in K. A negative W<sub>ideal</sub> means the unit produces work; the ideal output is −W<sub>ideal</sub>, the maximum possible. A positive W<sub>ideal</sub> is the minimum work input.

The same ideas are also called exergy or availability analysis. Do not confuse W<sub>ideal</sub> with a change in Gibbs free energy (thermodynamic property relations): ΔG uses the system temperature, not T₀.

blocks.where: W<sub>ideal</sub> is reversible work input in kJ (negative means work output); ΔH is outlet minus inlet enthalpy in kJ; ΔS is outlet minus inlet entropy in kJ/K; T₀ is dead-state temperature in K.

sections.h3: Gouy–Stodola: entropy generation becomes lost work

blocks.text: The second law gives the price of irreversibility. For any process, the total entropy generation is S<sub>gen</sub> = ΔS<sub>system</sub> + ΔS<sub>surroundings</sub>, with both changes in kJ/K. For an isolated composite system the surroundings term is already inside the system boundary and S<sub>gen</sub> is just the total entropy change. The Gouy–Stodola theorem states that W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>. S<sub>gen</sub> is in kJ/K and T₀ is in K, so W<sub>lost</sub> is in kJ. A reversible process has S<sub>gen</sub> = 0 and loses no work.

Lost work is also called exergy destruction. With work input positive, W<sub>lost</sub> = W<sub>actual</sub> − W<sub>ideal</sub>; this stays positive for turbines and compressors. For a turbine W<sub>ideal</sub> is more negative than W<sub>actual</sub>, so subtracting gives a positive loss. The lost work is always positive. Adding it to actual work is wrong; it is already gone.

Use T₀, not the hot or cold stream temperature, because the environment is the only free heat reservoir. If a plant rejects heat at 450 K but the outside air is at 300 K, the 300 K value sets the work value of that heat.

blocks.where: W<sub>lost</sub> is lost work in kJ; T₀ is dead-state temperature in K; S<sub>gen</sub> is total entropy generation in kJ/K.

examples.question: Heat of 1000 kJ passes from a reservoir at 500 K to a reservoir at 450 K. The surroundings are at 300 K. Find the entropy generated and the lost work. Treat the two reservoirs and the heat path as the system.
steps: Hot reservoir: ΔS<sub>hot</sub> = −Q/T<sub>hot</sub> = −1000 kJ / 500 K = −2.000 kJ/K.
Cold reservoir: ΔS<sub>cold</sub> = +Q/T<sub>cold</sub> = +1000 kJ / 450 K = +2.222 kJ/K.
The composite system is isolated, so S<sub>gen</sub> = ΔS<sub>hot</sub> + ΔS<sub>cold</sub> = −2.000 + 2.222 = 0.222 kJ/K.
Lost work: W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀ S<sub>gen</sub> = 300 K × 0.222 kJ/K = 66.7 kJ.
examples.answer: S<sub>gen</sub> = 0.222 kJ/K and W<sub>lost</sub> = 66.7 kJ; the heat transfer destroys 66.7 kJ of potential work.
examples.check:
Q = 1000.0
T_hot = 500.0
T_cold = 450.0
T0 = 300.0
dS_hot = -Q / T_hot
dS_cold = Q / T_cold
S_gen = dS_hot + dS_cold
W_lost = T0 * S_gen
print(round(S_gen, 3))
print(round(W_lost, 1))

examples.question: Use the steam turbine of the control-volume entropy balance: per kg, h falls from 3231.6 to 2530.0 kJ/kg and s rises from 6.9233 to 7.2679 kJ/(kg·K). Take T₀ = 300 K. Find W<sub>ideal</sub>, W<sub>actual</sub>, W<sub>lost</sub> and the second-law efficiency.
steps: W<sub>ideal</sub> = ΔH − T₀ΔS = −701.6 − 300 × 0.3446 = −701.6 − 103.4 = −805.0 kJ/kg: at best the steam could give 805.0 kJ/kg.
Adiabatic turbine: W<sub>actual</sub> = ΔH = −701.6 kJ/kg (it gives 701.6 kJ/kg).
W<sub>lost</sub> = W<sub>actual</sub> − W<sub>ideal</sub> = −701.6 − (−805.0) = 103.4 kJ/kg. Check: T₀S<sub>gen</sub> = 300 × 0.3446 = 103.4 kJ/kg.
Second-law efficiency = actual output / ideal output = 701.6/805.0 = 0.872.
examples.answer: W<sub>ideal</sub> = −805.0 kJ/kg, W<sub>actual</sub> = −701.6 kJ/kg, W<sub>lost</sub> = 103.4 kJ/kg and η<sub>II</sub> = 0.872.

traps: Do not add lost work to actual work. With work input positive, use W<sub>lost</sub> = W<sub>actual</sub> − W<sub>ideal</sub>; for a turbine this gives a positive loss because W<sub>actual</sub> is less negative than W<sub>ideal</sub>.
Use T₀, the environment temperature, not the hot reservoir or cold reservoir temperature, inside W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>.
S<sub>gen</sub> is total entropy generation for system plus surroundings. Using only the steam or gas entropy change misses the surroundings and gives the wrong lost work.
Check units: S<sub>gen</sub> in kJ/K times T₀ in K gives kJ. Mixing J/K with K gives a factor of 1000 error.

quiz.a: The temperature of the surroundings with which a stream can exchange heat reversibly; usually the ambient temperature.

quiz.q: Why does a reversible process have zero lost work?
quiz.a: A reversible process has S<sub>gen</sub> = 0, so W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀S<sub>gen</sub> = 0.

quiz.q: A process has S<sub>gen</sub> = 0.500 kJ/K. T₀ = 300 K. Find W<sub>lost</sub>.
A compressor uses W<sub>actual</sub> = 80 kJ. Its ideal work is 60 kJ. Find W<sub>lost</sub>.
quiz.a: Work is consumed: W<sub>lost</sub> = W<sub>actual</sub> − W<sub>ideal</sub> = 80 − 60 = 20 kJ.

quiz.q: A turbine gives W<sub>actual</sub> = 80 kJ; W<sub>ideal</sub> = 100 kJ. A student reports lost work as 180 kJ. Correct it.
quiz.a: Take work input as positive. For a turbine the given work values are outputs, so W<sub>actual</sub> = −80 kJ and W<sub>ideal</sub> = −100 kJ. Then W<sub>lost</sub> = W<sub>actual</sub> − W<sub>ideal</sub> = (−80) − (−100) = 20 kJ. The same 20 kJ is obtained using output magnitudes as W<sub>ideal</sub> − W<sub>actual</sub> = 100 − 80. The 180 kJ adds instead of subtracts.

quiz.q: Why is W<sub>lost</sub> calculated with T₀ rather than the hot reservoir temperature in the example?
quiz.a: T₀ is the only temperature at which heat is free and has no work value. The 500 K and 450 K reservoirs only fix S<sub>gen</sub>; the work that could have been made from the heat is measured against the surroundings, so W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Exergy analysis extends these ideas to every stream in a plant, giving second-law efficiency and pointing to where work is destroyed. Designers use it in pinch analysis, cryogenic liquefaction and data-centre cooling. Search 'exergy destruction', 'Gouy–Stodola theorem' and 'availability function'.
